summary: Summarizes principles for making future protocol transitions smoother and for planning them. Many protocols were not designed to allow easy replacement or extension, so changes like the introduction of IPv6 have been hard. It is informational guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: Replacing one protocol with another is mostly an economic problem, not a technical one. This document sets out what makes people actually switch, and what a plan for switching should say.

subtitle: Principles for smooth transitions between network protocols

tldr.problem: Some protocol changes go smoothly and others drag on for decades, because the people who would have to change rarely see a benefit for themselves.
tldr.mechanism: The document gathers the principles that make adoption work, distinguishes a flag-day switch from a long period of running both old and new, and lists the six things a good transition plan has to contain.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance rather than a specification, published by the Internet Architecture Board so that proposals to adopt a new protocol can be judged against a common set of criteria.

facts.label: Success principles from RFC 5218
facts.value: 4: incentive, incremental deployability, total cost and extensibility

today: RFC 8170 is an Informational document published by the Internet Architecture Board, with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the IAB's guidance on planning a transition. It asks the community to share what it learns on the architecture-discuss mailing list so that future documents on the topic can build on that experience.

sections.title: What a Transition Is and Why Some Fail
sections.content:
A transition is the process or period of changing from one state or condition to another. The document uses the term generically for the adoption of a new protocol where none existed before, the deployment of a new protocol that obsoletes a previous one, the deployment of an updated version of an existing protocol, and the decommissioning of an obsolete protocol. It focuses on technical transitions, though some principles may apply to organisational ones too.

Many IETF and IAB documents have discussed transitions. The IAB recommended that any technology for unilateral self-address fixing across NATs include an exit strategy to transition away from such a mechanism, and gave recommendations around internationalized domain names that led to the creation of the IETF Precis working group. Its statement on follow-up work on NAT-PT pointed out gaps in transitioning to IPv6 and resulted in the rechartering of the Behave working group.

More recently the IAB worked on more generally applicable principles. RFC 5218, on what makes for a successful protocol, studied the factors that contribute to and detract from the success of a protocol, and distinguished two kinds of transition: initial success, the move to the technology, and extensibility, the move to updated versions of it. Four principles from it are generally applicable to all technical transitions. The first is incentive: transition is easiest when the benefits come to those bearing the costs, so the benefits should outweigh the costs at each entity. Some successful cases did this by providing incentives such as tax breaks, by reducing costs such as freely available source code, by imposing the cost of not transitioning such as regulation, or by narrowing the scenarios of applicability to just the cases where benefits outweigh costs at all relevant entities. The second is incremental deployability: backwards compatibility makes transition easier, and transition is easiest when changing only one entity still benefits that entity. The third is total cost, which means considering costs beyond core hardware and software, such as operational tools and processes, personnel training, business model dependencies such as accounting and billing, and legal costs such as regulation and patents. The fourth is extensibility, designing for extensibility so that things can be fixed up later.

RFC 7305 reported on an IAB workshop on Internet Technology Adoption and Transition, which also discussed economic aspects. Two observations are worth repeating. The first is early-adopter incentives: part of Bitcoin's strategy was extra incentives for early adopters compared to late adopters, so providing a long-term advantage to early adopters can help stimulate transition even when the initial costs outweigh the initial benefit. The second is policy partners: policy-making organisations such as the Regional Internet Registries and ICANN can be important partners in enabling and facilitating transition.

The document's own case studies show both failure and partial success. Explicit Congestion Notification was standardized in 2001 and replaces loss as the only signal for detecting congestion, using an explicit signal first sent from a router to a recipient of a packet and reflected back to the sender. Its initial deployment in the early and mid 2000s led to severe problems with some network equipment, including home router crashes and reboots when packets with ECN flags were received, which led to firewalls stripping or dropping those packets and stalled deployment. The need for both endpoints to negotiate and support ECN and for on-path devices to mark traffic when congestion occurs, so that any benefit appears, was a further issue, and deployment across the Internet had failed. In the late 2000s, Linux and Windows servers began defaulting to passive ECN support, meaning they would negotiate ECN if asked by the client but would not ask to negotiate it by default. This was regarded as without risk, because only a client explicitly configured to negotiate ECN would surface connectivity problems. Gradually it increased server support from near zero in 2008 to 11% of the top million Alexa web servers in 2011, 30% in 2012 and 65% in late 2014, while the risk to connectivity of ECN negotiation reduced dramatically.
sections.plainLanguage: The main lesson from past transitions is that people change when it pays them to. If the cost sits with one group and the benefit with another, the change stalls. The document's example of congestion signalling shows a mechanism that worked technically but was blocked by equipment that crashed when it saw the new flags.

sections.title: Designing for the Next Change
sections.content:
Many protocols are designed to be extensible, using mechanisms such as options and version negotiation, to ease the transition to new features. However, implementations often succumb to commercial pressures to ignore that flexibility in favour of performance or economy, and as a result such extension mechanisms often experience problems in practice once they begin to be used. In other cases a mechanism might be put into a protocol for future use without an adequate sense of how it will be used, which causes problems later, as with SNMP's original security field or the IPv6 Flow Label. Designers therefore need to consider whether it would be easier to transition to a new protocol than it would be to ensure that an extension point is correctly specified and implemented so that it would be available when needed.

A protocol that plans for its own eventual replacement during its design makes later transitions easier, and developing and testing a design for the technical mechanisms needed to signal or negotiate a replacement is essential in such a plan.

When there is interest in translation between a new mechanism and an old one, the complexity of that translation must also be considered. The major challenge in translation is semantic differences: syntactic differences can often be translated seamlessly, semantic ones almost never. When designing for translatability, syntactic and semantic differences should therefore be clearly documented.

The HTTP case study shows what happens when a protocol outgrows its version number. During the development of HTTP/1.1 there was a fair amount of confusion regarding the semantics of HTTP version numbers, resulting in RFC 2145, and later it was felt that minor versioning caused more confusion than it was worth, so HTTP/2.0 became HTTP/2. That decision was informed by the observation that many implementations ignored the major version number of the protocol or misinterpreted it. As is the case with many protocol extension points, HTTP versioning had failed to be greased by use often enough and so had become rusted, so that only a limited range of values could interoperate. The same phenomenon has been observed in other protocols, such as TLS, and there are active efforts to identify extension points that need such grease and make them appear to be in use. Besides the protocol version, the HTTP extension points that are well greased include header fields, status codes, media types and cache-control extensions, while HTTP methods, content-encodings and chunk-extensions enjoy less flexibility and need to be extended more cautiously.
sections.plainLanguage: If a protocol leaves room for later changes, the room has to be used, or implementations stop trusting it. The document's advice is to design for your own replacement and to be honest about which differences between two protocols can be translated and which cannot.

sections.title: Switching at Once or Running Both
sections.content:
There is an important distinction between a strict flag-day style transition, where an old mechanism is immediately replaced with a new one, and a looser coexistence-based approach, where transition proceeds in stages with the new mechanism first added alongside the existing one for an overlap period and the old one removed later. When a new mechanism is backwards compatible with an existing one, transition is easiest, because different parties can transition at different times. When no backwards compatibility exists, as in the IPv4 to IPv6 transition, a plan must choose either a flag day or a period of coexistence. When a large number of entities are involved, a flag day becomes impractical or even impossible. Coexistence, on the other hand, involves the additional cost of maintaining two separate mechanisms during the overlap period, which could be quite long, and the longer the overlap, the more the old mechanism may get further deployment, increasing the overall pain of the transition.

Some new protocols or versions are developed with the intent of never retiring the protocol they replace, aiming only to address a subset of the use cases for which the original is used; for those, coexistence is the end state. Indefinite coexistence could be viable if removing the existing protocol is not an urgent goal, and it might also be necessary for wildly successful protocols that have more disparate uses than could reasonably be considered when designing a replacement. HTTP/2 does not aspire to cause the eventual decommissioning of HTTP/1.1 for these reasons.

The IPv6 case study shows how long this can take. Twenty-one years after the publication of the IPv6 specification in December 1995, the transition to IPv6 was still in progress. The first document to describe a transition plan was published less than a year after the protocol itself, and recommended coexistence, through dual-stack or tunnelling technology, with the expectation that over time all hosts would have IPv6 and IPv4 could be quietly retired. In the early stages, deployment was limited to peer-to-peer uses tunnelled over IPv4 networks, and the alignment of the cost of fixing the problem with the benefit allowed incremental benefits to those who used it. Operating system vendors had incentives, because with such tunnelling protocols they could get peer-to-peer applications working without depending on any infrastructure changes, which put the main IPv6 applications in the peer-to-peer category. Router vendors had some incentive, because IPv6 could be used within an intra-domain network more efficiently than tunnelling once the operating system vendors had IPv6 support and some special-purpose applications existed.

For content providers and ISPs, on the other hand, there was little incentive for deployment: there was no incremental benefit to deploying locally, since everyone already had IPv4 and there was no network effect benefit, and even as proponents argued that workarounds to extend the life of IPv4 made it more complex, IPv4 continued to work well enough for most applications. Workarounds to NAT problems included ICE, STUN and TURN, technologies that allowed those experiencing the problems to deploy solutions to resolve them, and as with end-to-end IPv6 tunnelling the incentives there aligned the cost of fixing the problem with the benefit. The IAB recommended that NAT technology proposals be considered short-term fixes and that proposals must include an exit plan so that they would decline over time, and it warned against generalising NAT solutions. In some ways these solutions, along with other IPv4 development, continued to reduce the incentive to deploy IPv6.

Some early advocates overstated the benefits of IPv6, suggesting that it had better security because IPsec was required, or that NAT was worse than it often appeared to be, or that IPv4 exhaustion would happen years sooner than it actually did. Some people pushed back on these exaggerations and decided that the protocol itself somehow lacked credibility. Not until a few years after IPv4 addresses were exhausted in various regional registry areas did IPv6 deployment significantly increase. The registries had been advocating IPv6 for some time, reducing fees for it and in some cases providing training, though there is little to suggest this had a significant effect; they and others conducted surveys of industries to learn why people did not deploy IPv6, which commonly listed lack of a business case, lack of training and lack of vendor support as primary hurdles.
sections.plainLanguage: You can switch everyone at once, but at Internet scale nobody can agree on the day. Running both is safer and slower, and the old one keeps gaining ground while it lasts. IPv6 shows how long that can go on: twenty-one years after the specification, the transition was still running.

sections.title: Where a Translator Belongs
sections.content:
A translation or adaptation mechanism is often required if the old and new mechanisms are not interoperable, and care must be taken when deciding whether one will work and where such a translator is best placed. A translation mechanism may not work for every use case: if translation from one protocol or version to another produces indeterminate results, translation will not work reliably. In addition, if translation always produces a downgraded protocol result, the incentive considerations of the plan become relevant.

Requiring a translator in the middle of the path can hamper end-to-end security and reliability, since the document points to the discussion of network-based filtering in RFC 7754. On the other hand, requiring a translation layer within an endpoint can be a resource issue in some cases, such as when the endpoint could be a constrained node.

When a translator is within an endpoint, it can attempt to hide the difference between an older protocol and a newer one, either by exposing one of the two sets of behaviour to applications and internally mapping it to the other, or by exposing a higher level of abstraction that is then alternatively mapped to either one depending on detecting which is needed. In contrast, when a translator is in the middle of the path, typically only the first approach can be done, since the middle of the path is typically unable to provide a higher level of abstraction.

Any transition strategy for a non-backwards-compatible mechanism should therefore include a discussion of where the incompatible mechanism is placed and a rationale, and the plan should also consider the transition away from the use of translation and adaptation technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old and new cannot talk to each other, something has to translate between them. Putting that translator in the middle of the network breaks end-to-end security; putting it inside every device uses resources that small devices may not have. The plan has to say which, and when the translator will go away.

sections.title: What a Good Transition Plan Contains
sections.content:
A review of the case studies suggests that a good transition plan includes at least six components: an understanding of what is already deployed and in use, an explanation of incentives for each entity involved, a description of the phases of the transition along with proposed criteria for each phase, a method for measuring the transition's success, a contingency plan for failure of the transition, and an effective method for communicating the plan to the entities involved and incorporating their feedback.

Existing deployment. An existing mechanism often has variations in implementations and operational deployments. A specification might include optional behaviours that may or may not be implemented or deployed, and there may be implementations that deviate from, or include vendor-specific extensions to, a specification. It is important to understand what variations one is intending to transition from or coexist with, since the technical and non-technical issues may vary greatly as a result.

Incentives. A plan should explain the incentives to each involved entity to support the transition. Many entities other than the endpoint applications and their users may be affected, and the barriers may be non-technical as well as technical. Network operations tools, practices and processes, personnel training, accounting and billing dependencies, and legal and regulatory incentives should all be considered. If there is opposition to a particular new protocol, from another standards organisation, a government or some other affected entity, various non-technical issues arise that should be part of what is planned. An analysis of incentives can be difficult and at times led astray by wishful thinking as opposed to adequately considering economic realities, so honestly considering any barriers to transition and justifying conclusions about others' incentives are key to a successful analysis.

Phases and criteria. Transition phases might include pilot or experimental deployment, coexistence, deprecation and removal phases. Timelines are notoriously difficult to predict and impossible to impose on uncoordinated transitions at the scale of the Internet, but rough estimates can sometimes help all involved entities understand the intended duration of each phase. More often it is useful to provide criteria that must be met in order to move to the next phase: whether removal is scheduled for a particular date, as with the Federal Communications Commission regulation to discontinue analog TV broadcasts in the United States by June 12, 2009, or whether removal is based on the use of the old mechanism falling below a specified level. RFC 5211 proposed a transition plan for IPv6 with a proposed timeline and criteria specific to each phase, and while the timeline was not accurately followed, the phases and timeline did serve as inputs to the World IPv6 Day and World IPv6 Launch events.

Measuring success. The degree of deployment of a given protocol or feature at a given phase can be measured differently depending on its design. Server-side protocols and options that identify themselves through a versioning or negotiation mechanism can be discovered through active Internet measurement studies.

Contingency planning. A contingency plan can be as simple as providing for indefinite coexistence between old and new, or for reverting to the old protocol until an updated version of the new one is available. Such a plan is useful if unforeseen problems are discovered during deployment, so that they can be quickly mitigated. World IPv6 Day included a contingency plan to revert to the original state at the end of the day, and after discovering no issues some participants found it unnecessary and kept the new state.

Communicating the plan. Many of the entities involved in a protocol transition may not be aware of the IETF or the RFC series, so dissemination through other channels is key for sufficiently broad communication. While flag days are impractical at Internet scale, coordinated events such as World IPv6 Launch may improve general awareness of an ongoing transition. There is also often a need for an entity facilitating the transition through advocacy and focus, independent of the IETF, which can be key in communicating the plan and its progress. Some transitions carry a risk of breaking backwards compatibility for some fraction of users, and when a transition affects competing entities facing the risk of losing customers to each other, there is an economic disincentive to transition; one role for a facilitating entity is to get competitors to transition during the same timeframe to mitigate this fear, and the success of World IPv6 Launch was largely due to ISOC playing this role.
sections.plainLanguage: A plan has to answer six questions: what is out there now, why each group should bother, what the stages are and what has to happen to move on, how you will know it worked, what you do if it goes wrong, and how everyone hears about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document discusses attributes of protocol transitions, and some types of transition can adversely affect security or privacy. Requiring a translator in the middle of the path may hamper end-to-end security and privacy, since it creates an attractive target.

In addition, coexistence of two protocols in general increases risk in the sense that it doubles the attack surface. It allows exploiters to choose the weaker of two protocols when both are available, or to force use of the weaker when negotiating between the protocols by claiming not to understand the stronger one.
sections.plainLanguage: Running two protocols at once means twice the ways in, and a translator in the middle of the network is a tempting target. Both are reasons to plan for the overlap period to end.

viz.caption: The two ways to move from one protocol to another

left.title: Flag day
left.desc: The old mechanism is replaced immediately. Only workable when the change is backwards compatible or when few entities are involved.

right.title: Coexistence
right.desc: The new mechanism runs alongside the old one for an overlap period, and the old one is removed later. Costs more, and the old one keeps gaining ground meanwhile.

viz.caption: The six components of a good transition plan

items.title: Existing deployment
items.text: What is already in use, including optional features and vendor-specific deviations.

items.title: Incentives
items.text: Why each involved entity should support the change, including non-technical barriers.

items.title: Phases and criteria
items.text: The stages of the transition and the conditions that must be met to move to the next one.

items.title: Measuring success
items.text: A method for finding out how far the transition has got at each phase.

items.title: Contingency planning
items.text: What to do if unforeseen problems appear, such as reverting or coexisting indefinitely.

items.title: Communicating the plan
items.text: How to reach the entities involved, and how to gather their feedback.
